key_concept: For a rigid body whose centre of mass is at rest (pure rotation about a fixed axis through the CM), the angular momentum is the same about every point: $\vec L_P = \vec L_{cm} + \vec r_{P\to cm} \times M\vec v_{cm}$ with $\vec v_{cm}=0$.
steps: Angular momentum about any point $P$ splits into two parts: $\vec L_P = \vec L_{\text{about CM}} + \vec r_{P\to cm}\times M\vec v_{cm}$.
The disc rotates about the vertical axis through its fixed centre $O$, which is also its centre of mass. So $\vec v_{cm}=0$.
The second (orbital) term therefore vanishes for every point $P$: $\vec r_{P\to cm}\times M\cdot 0 = 0$.
Hence $\vec L_A = \vec L_B = \vec L_O = I\omega\,\hat k$, where $I=\tfrac12 MR^2$. This holds irrespective of the distances $OA$ and $OB$.
Alternative check: the total linear momentum is $\vec p=\sum m_i\vec v_i = M\vec v_{cm}=0$. So $\vec L_A-\vec L_O = \vec r_{A\to O}\times\vec p = 0$.
why_not_others: Options (1), (2) and (4) assume that $L$ depends on the distance of the point, through factors like $r^2$ or $r$. That dependence appears only through the term $\vec r\times M\vec v_{cm}$, and this term is zero because the CM is at rest.
common_trap: Students apply the parallel-axis theorem ($I+Md^2$) for the points $A$ and $B$. But the disc does not rotate about axes through $A$ or $B$; it rotates about $O$, so its angular momentum is simply $I_O\omega$ about every point.
time_saving_tip: Zero total linear momentum means angular momentum is independent of the reference point. For pure rotation about the CM, answer 'same about all points' immediately.
